title: Day Around the Bay: SF King Tides Break 40-Year Record, With Higher Water Expected Wednesday
summary: SF’s king tides broke a November record, with more flooding expected Wednesday; a stabbing suspect surrendered after barricading inside a Lower Nob Hill apartment; and nearly 400 Waymos took shelter at the Cow Palace during last week’s storms.
content: Local: San Francisco’s waterfront saw its highest November tide in more than four decades Tuesday, with forecasters warning that Wednesday’s surge could bring even more extreme water levels and coastal flooding. [ ABC 7 ] A stabbing suspect was taken into custody Monday after barricading themselves inside an apartment in SF’s Lower Nob Hill, prompting a police response that included hostage negotiators and a tactical unit. [ Chronicle ] Nearly 400 Waymo robotaxis were sheltered overnight at San Francisco’s Cow Palace at least twice last week after heavy rain and flooding forced the company to halt service in the city. [ KRON4 ] National: Former Vice President Al Gore plans to purchase his hometown newspaper, the Carthage Courier in Tennessee, where he started his career as an Army journalist. [ Politico ] A Denver man is suspected of repeatedly blocking Waymo robotaxis with traffic cones before pelting them with eggs, with one investigator documenting 30 incidents involving the same suspect. [ 9News Denver ] New Army maps project a toxic lead dust plume drifting from that Iowa explosives plant into northeast Missouri during Wednesday’s planned detonation of five tons of degraded lead azide, which was postponed last week, raising concerns about potential contamination of farms and waterways. [ CBS News ] Video: Instagram user Rob Giannini captured stunning footage of the Outer Sunset during last week’s storm, noting how various species of birds continued gathering on the beach, feeding, watching the waves, and flying south through the pounding rain. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Rob Giannini (@robgofthebay)

title: FBI Releases Recording of Codefendant In Sheng Thao Trial as Defense Rests
summary: The federal corruption trial of former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao, her former romantic partner Andre Jones, and father-and-son businessmen David and Andy Duong is about to conclude, and a newly released audio recording reveals some new details in the prosecution's case.
content: The federal corruption trial of former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao, her former romantic partner Andre Jones, and father-and-son businessmen David and Andy Duong is about to conclude, and a newly released audio recording reveals some new details in the prosecution's case. The fates of Sheng Thao and her alleged co-conspirators will soon be in the hands of a jury, as the quartet of defendants are hoping for better outcomes than whatever they were likely offered as plea deals. The federal government's case contends that Thao and businessmen David and Andy Duong engaged in a yearslong scheme involving bribes, campaign contributions, and promises to help the Duongs' businesses. And Thao's romantic partner of recent years, with whom she is reportedly no longer together, Andre Jones, allegedly benefitted as well by way of what prosecutors characterized as a no-show consulting job at one of their companies. The star witness in the case was businessman and onetime partner of the Duongs, Mario Juarez, with whom they had a falling out around the time that federal agents raided the homes of Thao, Jones, and the Duongs in June 2024. Juarez took a plea in the case and testified against the Duongs about being a so-called "straw donor" for them, funneling money to Thao's 2022 campaign for mayor — money that, according to notes that investigators found on Andy Duong's iPhone, was part of a quid pro quo to get the City of Oakland to purchase some of the modular homes made from shipping containers being made by the Duongs' and Juarez's startup, Evolutionary Homes. The Duongs were also interested in having their waste management contract extended with the city — something that Thao also had influence over as a city councilmember — via their recycling company California Waste Solutions. As ABC 7 reports , the court released a new recording of Andy Duong sitting down for a three-hour interview with federal agents, without a lawyer present, in June 2024, days before they raided his home, and the home shared by Thao and Jones. In the recording, Duong can be heard saying that he had not spoken to Thao since she was elected over a year prior — despite his having hosted a trip to Vietnam that Thao went on in 2023. "It's like, come on. Now, you're the mayor, you don't even want to, you know, give me a high five?" Duong says, insinuating that Thao would not even acknowledge them, though they had known each other previously. The feds, clearly, already had some evidence, and an agent asks, "Was she, was she going to help you guys out with the, the container homes?" Duong replies, "No, nobody helped. Because the thing is, we. If we knew. So we have to establish, you know, a permit first, which we waiting for, the state permit." And, despite evidence that was presented at trial that the Duongs paid Andre Jones $85,000 of a promised $300,000 contract for consulting on Evolutionary Homes, Duong can be heard denying even knowing Jones. "And you have no knowledge of any money ever going to Jones?" the agent asks. "I have no knowledge at all," Duong says. "I never, you know, interact. I never meet Jones. I never gave him money. I never dealt with him all this time that I've seen him ever since, ever since I first seen him at City Hall." Closing arguments in the case are expected to begin next week, after the prosecution was set to call in a final witness today. Previously: Key Witness In Sheng Thao Corruption Trial Testifies About Alleged Pay-to-Play Deal

title: Macy’s and SF SPCA Celebrate 40 Years of Holiday Windows and Pet Adoptions
summary: Macy’s Union Square windows are once again filled with adoptable puppies and kittens, marking 40 years of a holiday tradition that has helped more than 10,000 shelter animals find homes.
content: Macy’s Union Square windows are once again filled with adoptable puppies and kittens, marking 40 years of a holiday tradition that has helped more than 10,000 shelter animals find homes. The SF SPCA hopes to find homes for 600 animals this holiday season, with adoptable puppies and kittens rotating through the windows as they find families, as Local News Matters reports . Three 2-month-old Chihuahua-mix puppies were reportedly among the first animals on display Friday, perking up as a crowd gathered outside Macy’s Union Square windows to catch a glimpse of them. One of the puppies had reportedly already been adopted by a new family by the time the annual Holiday Windows event got underway, and two black kittens were also scheduled to appear in the initial displays. View this post on Instagram A post shared by San Francisco SPCA (SFSPCA) (@sanfranciscospca) According to the SF Examiner , the tradition, now in its 40th year, began in 1987 at Gump’s under the leadership of former SF SPCA president Rich Avanzino, who died in September. The displays eventually moved to Macy’s, becoming a familiar part of the city's holiday season. More than 10,000 animals have reportedly found homes through Holiday Windows over the past four decades. SF SPCA CEO Dr. Jennifer Scarlett noted to the Examiner that if each animal lived for 10 years, that would represent 100,000 years of companionship. Planning for the event starts as early as March, with more than 100 staff members and 400 volunteers helping make the displays happen. Macy’s also presented the SF SPCA with a $5,000 donation during Friday's unveiling. The windows will be open Wednesdays through Sundays from noon to 5 pm through December 31, except Thanksgiving and Christmas. SF SPCA staff will be available at an adoption information station on Macy’s main floor to help interested visitors learn about the animals and adoption process. Daily livestreams of the puppies and kittens are also available on the SF SPCA website , from 9 am to 6 pm. The SF SPCA also provides accessible veterinary services, subsidized medical treatment, free vaccination clinics, and assistance for families struggling to afford care for their pets. Scarlett told the Examiner the organization provided more than $6 million in subsidized medical care this year, while finding homes for 4,700 dogs and cats. “Animal welfare isn’t simply about finding new homes,” she said. “Sometimes, it’s about keeping families together.” Previously: Those Puppies and Kittens Return to the Macy’s Union Square Windows for the Holiday Season This Friday

title: Extremely Detailed, Interactive Map of San Francisco Shows Moving Buses, Waymos, More
summary: A project to transform satellite images of San Francisco into an extraordinarily detailed, illustrated and animated map, complete with building-by-building clickable details and Muni buses on a live departure schedule, is a decent argument for the powers of AI image-making.
content: A project to transform satellite images of San Francisco into an extraordinarily detailed, illustrated and animated map, complete with building-by-building clickable details and Muni buses on a live departure schedule, is a decent argument for the powers of AI image-making. It's a far cry from the janky AI image generators of two years ago , which hallucinated bridges in San Francisco where they didn't belong and bizarre perspectives all around. It's called Small SF , and it calls itself a "live" map of San Francisco, which, in part, it is. Muni buses and ferries run on their actual schedules, weather conditions and the time of day are reflected in the lighting, and details down to the window sills of every building can be zoomed in on and examined. via Small SF There are some dated elements to the satellite images underpinning the whole thing — we still see you, Vaillancourt Fountain! — and the cars and Waymos you see roving about are just simulated at random intervals, not reflecting live traffic, obviously. The human behind all this is Ari Dutilh, a 21-year-old man from France who launched a program to support solo tech founders and also hosts an online photography lounge for sharing photographic work on Discord. As he tells SFist, he's been self-funding the map-building effort, which requires purchasing API credits on ChatGPT and Claude and rendering the city block by block using Google Earth's Photorealistic 3D Tiles. He says he was inspired by Isometric Seattle , which itself was traced using GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, but SmallSF is animated and even more detailed — click on any building a window will pop up giving specs like its construction date and height. Below you can see a side-by-side — get the full slider effect here — of the Google imagery on the left and the rendered illustration on the right. "The drawing keeps every building, street and parked car where it is, and the melted blobs of the render come back as actual trees," Dutilh explains. via Small SF More recently, Dutilh says he's received donations to fill in more of the map, with the city's west side having just been added in the last week — some areas around Lake Merced, as you may see, are beyond the zig-zag boundary of detail, and still show up as the blurrier tiles from Google Earth. "I've gotten emails from parents looking to donate and sharing how their kids are enjoying exploring the city on the website, people wanting to build additional features and functionality on top of the existing map, etc.," Dutilh tells us. "My favorite so far was a contribution from someone who requested we capture (and preserve) The Box Shop — an artist's collective [and original home of Entwined ] in Bayview that will soon be torn down and converted into condos." And, Dutilh says, he imagines the map will have more utility beyond just being a novelty for locals and tourists. Some users are already putting it to use just to keep track of transit schedules. "People are already using it to monitor their bus/BART/Muni stop by their home or office, either by keeping the tab open in their browser or using the TV mode," Dutilh says. "In fact, someone emailed me letting me know they created an entire Firestick TV/Amazon TV app that converts the website into a navigable TV app." That same person, Dutilh says, is hoping to get his apartment building to feature the live map on a screen in the lobby. Just to prove the point about the on-time Muni tracking, Dutilh took a photo of a live 33-Ashbury/18th Street pulling up to a stop at Valencia and 18th last night, and the simultaneous animated bus pulling up on the Small SF map. Photo by Ari Dutilh Go forth and have some map fun... [ Small SF ]

title: Man Convicted of Hate Crime For Shouting Epithets at Elderly Black Woman In Laurel Heights
summary: A 55-year-old San Francisco man has been convicted of a hate crime after verbally attacking a woman who asked him to put out his cigarette outside a Peet's Coffee shop in Laurel Heights.
content: A 55-year-old San Francisco man has been convicted of a hate crime after verbally attacking a woman who asked him to put out his cigarette outside a Peet's Coffee shop in Laurel Heights. The incident happened outside the Laurel Village Peet's location on the 3400 block of California Street — and the date of the incident was not immediately available in public records. According to the SF District Attorney's Office and evidence that prosecutors presented at trial, 55-year-old Mohd Said Alqdimat was sitting outside the coffee shop smoking a cigarette when an 82-year-old woman approached while on her morning walk with her 86-year-old husband. The woman, who suffers from asthma, asked Alqdimat if he would kind extinguish his cigarette, to which he responded angrily. According to investigators, Alqdimat "stood up, approached the victim to within arm’s reach, and began yelling racial slurs at her." This included repeated use of the N-word, and threats to physically attack the woman if she did not leave the vicinity. The victim said that she and her husband feared for their safety and were shaken by the incident for days afterward. Alqdimat was later arrested and charged with a hate crime — technically misdemeanor interference with civil rights by threat — and he was convicted this week on that charge. "No one should be made to feel unsafe in their own community because of the color of their skin,” said District Attorney Brooke Jenkins in a statement. "Racially motivated threats and intimidation have no place in San Francisco, and my office will continue to hold accountable those who target others with hate and violence." Jenkins added, "I commend the jury for recognizing the seriousness of this conduct and standing up for the dignity and civil rights of every member of our community." Alqdimat will be sentenced on December 1, and he faces up to one year in jail and a $5,000 fine.

title: SF Man Says He Found Loaded Handgun Inside Waymo, With Bullet In Chamber
summary: A San Francisco resident says he initially mistook a Colt .25 handgun for a novelty lighter when he got into his Waymo in North Beach, only to discover it was loaded, with a round in the chamber.
content: A San Francisco resident says he initially mistook a Colt .25 handgun for a novelty lighter when he got into his Waymo in North Beach, only to discover it was loaded, with a round in the chamber. Stefano Scalia, an SF resident and former firearms instructor, said he discovered the handgun on the floor of a Waymo after taking a ride from North Beach to Cole Valley. The Colt .25 initially looked like a novelty lighter, he said, but turned out to be loaded, with a round in the chamber. Scalia said he made the weapon safe before reporting the incident. The handgun had a grip safety, which Scalia said meant it could have fired if someone, including a child, picked it up and pulled the trigger. Photos Scalia shared alongside his post show the handgun on the Waymo's back seat, as well as police officers investigating the vehicle. Fuck it I’m posting. I got a @Waymo in north beach back to Cole Valley and when I got in what I thought was a novelty lighter was a loaded handgun - a colt .25. I was a firearms instructor so I rendered the gun safe. There was a round in the chamber. The colt .25 has a grip safety meaning if a kid or someone picked this up and pulled the trigger it would have fired. Waymo, even though I’m a rider with over 800 rides, gave me two free rides. I don’t think I can support this company anymore. — Stefano (@stefanoscalia) November 25, 2026 Scalia, who said he has taken more than 800 rides with Waymo, was offered two free rides by the company in response to his complaint. He said the company's email responses were so dismissive that he no longer felt comfortable supporting the service. The post, shared by the Instagram account Real Bay Area Memes , drew a mix of jokes and criticism. “The most shocking part to me is trusting Waymo 800x,” said one commenter. Another commenter pointed out the frequency of gun ownership in the US. “Person accidentally drops their gun in a cab in a country where guns are everywhere. Shocking,” they said. As SFist reported in September, Waymo previously alerted police after two juveniles allegedly brought an AR-style ghost rifle into one of its vehicles in the Outer Richmond. The two now face charges related to illegal firearm possession. Related: Pair of Juveniles Arrested After Waymo Reports 'AR-Style' Ghost Gun to SFPD

title: SF’s Housing Shortfall Could Mean Taller Buildings and More Upzoning Across the City
summary: San Francisco has issued just 7,000 of the 29,000 building permits required by January 2027, prompting YIMBY advocates to push for taller buildings, fewer development restrictions, and more aggressive neighborhood upzoning.
content: San Francisco has issued just 7,000 of the 29,000 building permits expected by the state by January 2027, prompting YIMBY advocates to push for taller buildings, fewer development restrictions, and more aggressive neighborhood upzoning. At a recent meeting at Eureka Valley Community Center, about 20 housing advocates discussed the changes San Francisco will have to make after it misses its January 31, 2027 deadline, as Mission Local reports . The city has reportedly issued roughly 7,000 building permits toward a target of 29,000, part of California's requirement that San Francisco accommodate 82,000 new homes between 2023 and 2031. Under Program 8.1.5 of the city's Housing Element, missing the interim target requires San Francisco to return to the drawing board and enact additional rezoning and reductions in constraints on housing projects. The city must develop enough additional capacity to account for 115% of its shortfall, and the revised policies must receive state approval by July 31, 2028. The current mandate dates back to 2022, when the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) launched an unprecedented review of San Francisco's housing approval process and development pipeline, as SFist reported at the time. The department cited some of the longest project-approval timelines and highest construction costs in the state, along with receiving more complaints about San Francisco than any other California jurisdiction. Housing advocates had already warned that the city's projected development pipeline was overly optimistic, and that officials were avoiding politically unpopular zoning changes in some of the city's least-dense neighborhoods, particularly on the west side. The Board of Supervisors unanimously passed the Housing Element in January 2023, and the state approved it the following month. But the city's slow progress continued. By June 2023, San Francisco was approving an average of just eight new housing units per month , prompting HCD to warn that the city was not following through on its commitments, as SFist reported previously. “A housing element is not a paper exercise,” the department wrote in a letter to the Planning Commission at the time. “It is an enforceable commitment to the state that a city or county would take specific actions on specific timeframes over an eight-year period.” According to Mission Local, the consequences of failing to meet the current interim target are different from the earlier threat of losing state approval for the Housing Element. This time, the city is required to adopt additional measures to make up for its shortfall, with the state overseeing approval of the revised policies. YIMBY advocates reportedly want to influence what those measures look like, including allowing taller buildings on residential streets and in neighborhoods such as Bernal Heights and Potrero Hill that were largely untouched by the city's previous upzoning plan . They also want to extend height increases along commercial corridors, where the city raised limits from four stories to six or eight stories in December 2025. Some construction costs, including higher interest rates and increased material prices tied to federal tariffs, are outside the city's control, per Mission Local. But housing advocates say San Francisco can make building more financially feasible by reducing local taxes and regulatory barriers. San Francisco has already begun easing some of the costs and requirements associated with new housing. In July, the Board of Supervisors temporarily reduced the city's inclusionary affordable-housing requirement for qualifying developments from 15% to 5% , while also reducing certain development impact fees. The change was intended to make more projects financially feasible and encourage construction. Mayor Daniel Lurie and Supervisor Bilal Mahmood have also proposed cutting the city's transfer tax on large real estate transactions, which developers say makes financing new projects more difficult. Their proposal, revived this month as the BUILD Act, would lower the tax on sales of properties worth more than $10 million and exempt the first sale of certain newly constructed multifamily buildings. The proposal has not yet been enacted. YIMBY Action's Bay Area organizing director Brandon Powell said advocates intend to help shape the city's response and persuade the mayor's administration that more ambitious housing policies are politically worthwhile. Previously: Much of Bay Area Lagging Far Behind Even SF on State-Mandated Housing Goals

title: Thanksgiving Eve Headlines: Sunny After All
summary: The rain seems to have already passed and pre-Thanksgiving travel is going smoothly at the airports; authorities are seeking help identifying a man found dead in SoMa; and Trump announced a new round of tariffs.
content: Despite the terrible forecast, it seems like all the rain came overnight, and it's sunny and clear around the Bay and should stay this way all day. The king tides were expected to peak around 10:50 am Wednesday, but all seems to be going smoothly at SFO and Oakland Airport. [ KTVU ] Here are some photos from KRON4 of the tides breaching the seawall on the Embarcadero Tuesday. The San Francisco Office of the Chief Medical Examiner is seeking the public's help in identifying a man who was found dead on the sidewalk last week in SoMa, who was approximately 60 years old. [ KRON4 ] San Francisco police arrested a suspect on suspicion of stabbing and injuring someone in an apartment building on the 900 block of Sutter Street Monday morning. [ Chronicle ] Defense attorneys for David Duong in the Sheng Thao corruption trial filed a last-ditch motion to have the case dismissed, arguing that prosecution witness Mario Juarez gave false testimony. [ ABC 7 ] Of course, we now know that President Trump holds of tens of millions of dollars in Nvidia stock in his personal portfolio, giving him plenty of reason to press the company's board to reinstate Jensen Huang. [ CBS News ] Trump announced a new round of tariffs on goods from 14 major trading partners, including China, Brazil, and the European Union, just as he faces a hostile incoming Congress and mounting frustration over tariffs among voters. title: Video: Waves Take Out Section of Pacifica Municipal Pier
summary: High, pounding surf at high tide Wednesday morning brought more flooding to the coastal town of Pacifica — as well as taking out part of its municipal pier — and evacuations were ordered for some homes in Stinson Beach as well.
content: High, pounding surf at high tide Wednesday morning brought more flooding to the coastal town of Pacifica — as well as taking out part of its municipal pier — and evacuations were ordered for some homes in Stinson Beach as well. This morning's storm and king tides plus El Niño brought massive waves to the coast, including at SF's Ocean Beach, where emergency sand-moving work was happening Wednesday to shore up dunes that were being eroded. Down in Pacifica, for the second time in a little over a week, floodwaters inundated homes and parts of the town, and around 11 am, a large wave took out the end section of the L-shaped Pacifica Municipal Pier. Two videos below captured the collapse, one from Colin McCarthy of the Xitter account @US_StormWatch, and one from ABC 7's helicopter. Oh my god, part of the Pacifica Pier just collapsed. https://t.co/dSsvW7dXpP — Colin McCarthy (@US_Stormwatch) November 25, 2026 #BREAKING: A massive wave took out part of the Pacifica pier as the powerful waves from peak king tides battered the coast and flooded streets and homes. Latest here: https://t.co/tvD9pX1MEu https://t.co/9BTgZJuXIy — ABC7 News (@abc7newsbayarea) November 25, 2026 The pier, which is around 50 years old, was already temporarily closed to the public due to structural issues from storm damage in 2024, and a beloved cafe at its base, the Chit Chat Cafe, was demolished back in June . Photos elsewhere show helpless residents by the shoreline in Pacifica either trying to move or pump pooling water or simply assessing the damage. KRON4 has images from an AP photographer showing residents Dante Campagna and his father Dino Campagna dealing with an apartment — which they just moved into a month ago — that had what appeared to be at least six inches of water in it, as they tried to salvage their belongings. As the Chronicle reports , the water began inundating the area south of the pier, at least a block in from the shoreline in the Sharp Park neighborhood, around 9 am Wednesday. "Trash cans floated amid seafoam. Trash cans floated amid seafoam," the paper says. Waves flood over a sea wall on November 25, 2026 in Pacifica, California. Novembers "King Tides" in the Bay Area are being amplified by El Niño conditions. (Photo by Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images) Floodwater fills a street on November 25, 2026 in Pacifica, California. Novembers "King Tides" in the Bay Area are being amplified by El Niño conditions. (Photo by Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images) Jarret Morgan carries a hose through floodwater on November 25, 2026 in Pacifica, California. Novembers "King Tides" in the Bay Area are being amplified by El Niño conditions. (Photo by Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images) Pedestrians stand as a wave breaks over a sea wall on November 25, 2026 in Pacifica, California. Novembers "King Tides" in the Bay Area are being amplified by El Niño conditions. (Photo by Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images) Up in Stinson Beach, on the Marin County coast, some residents were told to shelter in place after evacuation orders were given Wednesday morning for the most flood-prone homes. stinson beach king tides this morning https://t.co/Xs8Pdlel4j — Dylan Mitic (@DylanMitic) November 25, 2026 Per the Chronicle, rising floodwaters were also seen in Mill Valley and Marin City Wednesday afternoon.

title: [Update] War Memorial Director Resigns Following Whistleblower Report
summary: SF’s War Memorial director is on paid leave amid a city investigation into allegations that she used an affiliated nonprofit to bypass contracting rules and retaliated against employees who raised concerns by laying them off.
content: SF’s War Memorial director has resigned after being on paid leave amid a city investigation into allegations that she used an affiliated nonprofit to bypass contracting rules and retaliated against employees who raised concerns by laying them off. Kate Sofis, managing director of the San Francisco War Memorial and Performing Arts Center, had been on paid leave since November 13 as the city investigated allegations that she used an affiliated nonprofit to bypass city contracting and hiring rules, as Mission Local reports . The city-owned cultural institution includes the War Memorial Opera House, as well as Davies Symphony Hall, the Herbst Theatre, and Wilsey Center, among other performance spaces. On Wednesday evening, Sofis resigned from her post, per Mission Local . Two whistleblowers reportedly filed separate complaints this spring alleging Sofis used the SF Performing Arts Center Foundation, an affiliated nonprofit that employs event staff and handles some of the center's finances, as a pass-through for expenses that would otherwise require city approval. Documents reviewed by Mission Local show that consultants hired through the foundation billed the city at least $195,000 through March. Some received monthly retainers rather than payment for specific projects, with the complaints questioning the lack of defined work, deliverables, and performance measures. According to Mission Local, the complaints also question a $4,762 charge that Sofis billed the foundation for a four-day Los Angeles trip, airfare for two European trips she had not yet taken, and a laptop. Documents show she left those expenses off a reimbursement accounting requested by a foundation board member. Separately, two foundation board members reportedly resigned this summer over financial concerns, including John Caldon, the War Memorial's managing director from 2019 to 2023 and later the foundation's treasurer. In his resignation letter, Caldon said financial information provided by department management was “incomplete and inaccurate.” The whistleblowers also allege Sofis retaliated against them by including them both on a list of city employees to be laid off last spring, per Mission Local. The complaints say consultants hired through the foundation effectively took over similar work. The War Memorial's 11-member Board of Trustees, whose members are appointed by the mayor and who have the authority to hire and fire the managing director, reportedly held a special meeting Tuesday to evaluate Sofis's performance. The 85-minute meeting was reportedly attended by San Francisco Inspector General Alex Shepard and Deputy City Attorneys Keslie Stewart and Lauren Curry. The board voted not to disclose what was discussed, but Mission Local reports that another special meeting was scheduled for next Monday. Mayor Daniel Lurie reportedly learned of the allegations about two weeks ago and asked the board to convene. Sofis was appointed in May 2023 after serving as director of then-Mayor London Breed's Office of Economic and Workforce Development. As Mission Local reported at the time, her appointment followed lobbying by Breed's staff , who reportedly told employees she would be “staying within the city family.” Trustee Quentin Kopp questioned the appointment at the time, noting that Sofis had no prior performing arts experience — a stated requirement for the position, later surmising that, “City Hall needed a place for her.” According to Mission Local, Sofis was chosen over candidates with extensive industry backgrounds , including one who spent 13 years as a director at the San Francisco Symphony and another who worked six years at the San Francisco Opera and a decade managing ballet companies, including the San Francisco Ballet. Other applicants had held management roles at venues and organizations including the Tennessee Performing Arts Center, Royal Shakespeare Company, Madison Center for the Arts, the Fillmore, the Vogue Theater, and the Marsh. One had even worked on the set of Oprah Winfrey’s talk show. Sofis reportedly earned $330,670, including benefits, in 2025. As SFist reported earlier this year, she was also responsible for getting the lights turned back on during last year's infamous PG&E blackout so Mayor Lurie's daughter's Nutcracker performance could go on as planned, which sparked some controversy. Prior to her roles at SF War Memorial and the Office of Economic and Workforce Development, Sofis was co-founder and CEO of local manufacturing nonprofit, SFMade . Related: There’s Fresh Friction Between Lurie and PG&E Over Day-of-Blackout ‘Nutcracker’ Performance

title: Willie Brown Launches Shots Across the Bow at Kamala, Says She 'Doesn't Have It' to Be Prez
summary: Perhaps this shouldn't be a surprise, but old Willie Brown has some forthright opinions about the Democratic field heading into the presidential election cycle that will kick off next year, and he will not be backing his long ago ex Kamala Harris.
content: Perhaps this shouldn't be a surprise, but old Willie Brown has some forthright opinions about the Democratic field heading into the presidential election cycle that will kick off next year, and he will not be backing his long ago ex Kamala Harris if she should decide to run again. Speaking to journalist Tara Palmeri at the weekly Saturday John's Grill lunch that he regularly attends, Willie Brown did not mince words about his thoughts on Kamala Harris's prospects in 2028 — an opinion that he has shared previously. "I’m sorry that she even thinks about running for president. I don’t want her to run," Brown told Palmeri, in no uncertain terms. He suggests that she should have leveraged her notoriety to, perhaps, take a gig with CBS or ABC News, or wait her turn to become a Supreme Court justice. But running again for the White House? "She's not a communicator," Brown says. "She doesn't have it... [She has] no Baptist preacher flavor in her soul." Clearly Brown would like to telegraph the message to Harris, if he hadn't already, that she should step aside and let his well groomed protégé Gavin Newsom take a shot. All the way back in June, Brown was going on television to tell Kamala not to run. As he told ABC News , Harris is "the most recent loser" in the minds of the country, and "When you embrace somebody for the job, you really want to embrace a winner.” Brown added, “And Newsom would be what you would have to say at the moment is a winner." Is he, though? Newsom has some skeletons in the old closet that will no doubt come up in a national race, and it's a little hard to imagine, even after that "Blue tsunami," that the majority of the country would want a well-heeled California Democrat leading the country, no matter how presidential Newsom has always seemed. A mid-November Reuters poll of Democratic voters had Newsom and Harris neck and neck, each with 23% support, but they both were behind Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and previous presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg, who each pulled in 29% in the poll. Neither Harris nor Newsom, nor the other two for that matter, have officially declared their candidacy for 2028. Sidebar: The California Post really went for it in their headline, picking up Palmeri's interview with Brown, which is "Kamala Harris' much older ex-lover deals crushing blow to her 2028 White House ambitions."
